source_evidence.anchor: standing rectangular full-rank setup immediately before equation (1)
source_evidence.observation: The paper assumes a real m-by-n matrix A with m >= n and rank(A) = n. It writes A = QR in exact arithmetic, with Q having orthonormal columns and R an n-by-n upper-triangular nonsingular matrix.

Algorithm 2 computes s_k = Q_(k-1)^T a_k, v_k = a_k - Q_(k-1)s_k, psi_k = ||a_k||_2, phi_k = ||s_k||_2, r_kk = (psi_k - phi_k)^(1/2)(psi_k + phi_k)^(1/2), and q_k = v_k/r_kk. It is explicitly named the Cholesky-like or pythagorean classical Gram-Schmidt algorithm, CGS-P.

source_evidence.anchor: IEEE floating-point model and linear approximation
source_evidence.observation: The paper assumes IEEE floating-point arithmetic and states fl(x+y) = (x+y)(1+delta), |delta| <= epsilon_M, for results in the normalized range. It adopts (1+epsilon_M)^(p(n)) = 1+p(n)epsilon_M+O(epsilon_M^2) for modest p(n), treating second-order terms as insignificant.

source_evidence.anchor: numbered equation (2), visually inspected typeset radicals
source_evidence.observation: The typeset equation defines c1(m,1)=1 and c1(m,k)=2*sqrt(2)*m*k+2*sqrt(k) for k=2,...,n. Visual inspection shows that the first square-root bar covers only the numeral 2, while the second covers only k; it does not state sqrt(2*m*k). It also defines c2(m,1)=m+2, c2(m,k)=3.5*m*k^2-1.5*m*k+16*k for k=2,...,n, c3(m,k)=0.5*c2(m,k), and c4(m,k)=c2(m,k)+2*c1(m,k).

For the R produced by Algorithm 2, Theorem 1 assumes c4(m,k)epsilon_M*kappa_2(R_k)^2 < 1 for every k, where kappa_2(R_k)=||R_k||_2||R_k^(-1)||_2. For k=1,...,n and up to O(epsilon_M^2), it states equations (4)-(8), including ||I-Q_k^T Q_k||_2 <= c4(m,k)kappa_2(R_k)^2 epsilon_M.

The paper says condition (3) assures that R is nonsingular and that bounds (7) and (8) hold. Remark 1 emphasizes that condition (3) and bound (7) are stated in terms of kappa_2(R_k), although a variation can be related to kappa_2(A_k).

The proof uses Q_k=(A_k+Delta A_k)R_k^(-1) and the exact identity I-Q_k^T Q_k = R_k^(-T)(E_k-A_k^T Delta A_k-(Delta A_k)^T A_k-(Delta A_k)^T Delta A_k)R_k^(-1). Applying bounds (4)-(6) gives the first-order coefficient c2(m,k)+2*c1(m,k)=c4(m,k), with the remaining terms absorbed into O(epsilon_M^2).

binders: Inherited binders are integers m,n with m >= n and a real m-by-n matrix A of rank n. (PDF p. 2, anchor: standing rectangular full-rank setup immediately before equation (1)).
The theorem ranges over k=1,...,n and defines A_k as the first k columns of A. (PDF p. 4, anchor: Theorem 1, condition (3) and conclusions (4)-(8)).
R_k and Q_k are the computed partial factors after processing k columns with Algorithm 2. (PDF p. 3, anchor: Algorithm 2 (CGS-P)).
For each k, equations (4)-(6) introduce the error matrices Delta A_k and E_k and the scalar mu_k. (PDF p. 4, anchor: Theorem 1, condition (3) and conclusions (4)-(8)).
hypotheses: A is a full-column-rank real m-by-n matrix with m >= n and rank(A)=n; this is inherited from the standing setup rather than repeated in Theorem 1. (PDF p. 2, anchor: standing rectangular full-rank setup immediately before equation (1)).

R and Q are the floating-point results of Algorithm 2, CGS-P, using the pythagorean diagonal formula. (PDF p. 3, anchor: Algorithm 2 (CGS-P); PDF p. 4, anchor: Theorem 1, condition (3) and conclusions (4)-(8)).
The arithmetic is IEEE floating-point arithmetic with machine unit epsilon_M, under the stated normalized-range model. (PDF p. 3, anchor: IEEE floating-point model and linear approximation).
For every k=1,...,n, c4(m,k)epsilon_M*kappa_2(R_k)^2 < 1. (PDF p. 4, anchor: Theorem 1, condition (3) and conclusions (4)-(8)).

The conclusions are interpreted to first order, with terms of order O(epsilon_M^2) omitted. (PDF p. 3, anchor: IEEE floating-point model and linear approximation; PDF p. 4, anchor: Theorem 1, condition (3) and conclusions (4)-(8)).
conclusions: For every k=1,...,n, Q_k R_k - A_k = Delta A_k and ||Delta A_k||_2 <= c1(m,k)||A_k||_2 epsilon_M, to within O(epsilon_M^2). (PDF p. 4, anchor: Theorem 1, condition (3) and conclusions (4)-(8), equation (4)).

For every k=1,...,n, R_k^T R_k - A_k^T A_k = E_k and ||E_k||_2 <= c2(m,k)||A_k||_2^2 epsilon_M, to within O(epsilon_M^2). (PDF p. 4, anchor: Theorem 1, condition (3) and conclusions (4)-(8), equation (5)).
For every k=1,...,n, ||R_k||_2 = ||A_k||_2(1+mu_k), with |mu_k| <= c3(m,k)epsilon_M, to within O(epsilon_M^2). (PDF p. 4, anchor: Theorem 1, condition (3) and conclusions (4)-(8), equation (6)).
For every k=1,...,n, ||I-Q_k^T Q_k||_2 <= c4(m,k)kappa_2(R_k)^2 epsilon_M, to within O(epsilon_M^2). (PDF p. 4, anchor: Theorem 1, condition (3) and conclusions (4)-(8), equation (7)).
For every k=1,...,n, ||Q_k||_2 <= sqrt(2), to within O(epsilon_M^2). (PDF p. 4, anchor: Theorem 1, condition (3) and conclusions (4)-(8), equation (8)).
The paper additionally states that condition (3) assures nonsingularity of R and validity of conclusions (7) and (8). (PDF p. 4, anchor: paragraph after Theorem 1 and Remark 1).
definitions_and_conventions: A=(a_1,...,a_n), Q=(q_1,...,q_n), and R=(r_jk). (PDF p. 2, anchor: standing rectangular full-rank setup immediately before equation (1)).
Algorithm 2 initializes r_11=||a_1||_2, q_1=a_1/r_11, R_1=(r_11), and Q_1=(q_1). (PDF p. 3, anchor: Algorithm 2 (CGS-P)).

For k=2,...,n, Algorithm 2 sets s_k=Q_(k-1)^T a_k, v_k=a_k-Q_(k-1)s_k, psi_k=||a_k||_2, phi_k=||s_k||_2, r_kk=(psi_k-phi_k)^(1/2)(psi_k+phi_k)^(1/2), and q_k=v_k/r_kk. (PDF p. 3, anchor: Algorithm 2 (CGS-P)).
R_k is formed by adjoining s_k and r_kk to R_(k-1), while Q_k is formed by adjoining q_k to Q_(k-1). (PDF p. 3, anchor: Algorithm 2 (CGS-P)).
A_k is the matrix consisting of the first k columns of A, and kappa_2(R_k)=||R_k||_2||R_k^(-1)||_2. (PDF p. 4, anchor: Theorem 1, condition (3) and conclusions (4)-(8)).
implicit_context: From the standing setup and Algorithm 2, A_k and Q_k are m-by-k matrices and R_k is k-by-k upper triangular. (PDF p. 2, anchor: standing rectangular full-rank setup immediately before equation (1); PDF p. 3, anchor: Algorithm 2 (CGS-P)).

The identity matrix I in equation (7) has the implicit k-by-k dimension required by Q_k^T Q_k; the paper does not write a subscript on I. (PDF p. 4, anchor: Theorem 1, condition (3) and conclusions (4)-(8)).
A_k denotes input data, whereas Q_k and R_k are explicitly described as computed matrices. (PDF p. 4, anchor: Theorem 1, condition (3) and conclusions (4)-(8)).

The full-rank rectangular setup is inherited by Theorem 1 even though the theorem itself begins directly with the floating-point and condition-number assumptions. (PDF p. 2, anchor: standing rectangular full-rank setup immediately before equation (1); PDF p. 4, anchor: Theorem 1, condition (3) and conclusions (4)-(8)).
statement.algorithm_linkage: The result is linked specifically to Algorithm 2, the Cholesky-like pythagorean classical Gram-Schmidt algorithm CGS-P. Its diagonal is the product sqrt(psi_k-phi_k)*sqrt(psi_k+phi_k), not the standard CGS-S choice ||v_k||_2. The paper explicitly says the preceding Algorithm 1 lemma is not correct as stated and replaces it with Theorem 1 for Algorithm 2. (PDF p. 3, anchor: Algorithm 2 (CGS-P)).
numerical_model: The paper assumes floating-point arithmetic satisfying the IEEE standard. (PDF p. 3, anchor: IEEE floating-point model and linear approximation).
It explicitly states fl(x+y)=(x+y)(1+delta), with |delta|<=epsilon_M, for results in the normalized range. (PDF p. 3, anchor: IEEE floating-point model and linear approximation).

It uses the linear approximation (1+epsilon_M)^(p(n))=1+p(n)epsilon_M+O(epsilon_M^2) for modest p(n), assuming the second-order contribution is insignificant. (PDF p. 3, anchor: IEEE floating-point model and linear approximation).
Theorem 1 labels Q_k and R_k as computed matrices and states its bounds only to within O(epsilon_M^2). (PDF p. 4, anchor: Theorem 1, condition (3) and conclusions (4)-(8)).
error_notions: Delta A_k is a factorization residual defined by Q_k R_k-A_k=Delta A_k and bounded relative to ||A_k||_2. (PDF p. 4, anchor: Theorem 1, condition (3) and conclusions (4)-(8), equation (4)).

E_k is a normal-equations or Gram-matrix residual defined by R_k^T R_k-A_k^T A_k=E_k and bounded relative to ||A_k||_2^2. (PDF p. 4, anchor: Theorem 1, condition (3) and conclusions (4)-(8), equation (5)).
mu_k measures the relative perturbation between ||R_k||_2 and ||A_k||_2. (PDF p. 4, anchor: Theorem 1, condition (3) and conclusions (4)-(8), equation (6)).
Loss of column orthogonality is measured by ||I-Q_k^T Q_k||_2. (PDF p. 4, anchor: Theorem 1, condition (3) and conclusions (4)-(8), equation (7)).
The proof derives the orthogonality error from E_k and Delta A_k through an exact inverse-sandwich identity. (PDF p. 14, anchor: Appendix proof of equation (7)).
norms: All theorem bounds use the paper's 2-norm notation ||.||_2. (PDF p. 4, anchor: Theorem 1, condition (3) and conclusions (4)-(8)).
Algorithm 2 uses ||a_k||_2 and ||s_k||_2 in the pythagorean diagonal computation. (PDF p. 3, anchor: Algorithm 2 (CGS-P)).
The condition number is kappa_2(R_k)=||R_k||_2||R_k^(-1)||_2, and equation (7) uses its square. (PDF p. 4, anchor: Theorem 1, condition (3) and conclusions (4)-(8)).
The orthogonality error is a matrix 2-norm of I-Q_k^T Q_k, not an entrywise or Frobenius norm. (PDF p. 4, anchor: Theorem 1, condition (3) and conclusions (4)-(8)).
constants_and_indexing: c1(m,1)=1; for k=2,...,n, c1(m,k)=2*sqrt(2)*m*k+2*sqrt(k). The first radical contains only 2, and the second contains only k. (PDF p. 4, anchor: numbered equation (2), visually inspected typeset radicals).
c2(m,1)=m+2; for k=2,...,n, c2(m,k)=3.5*m*k^2-1.5*m*k+16*k. (PDF p. 4, anchor: numbered equation (2), visually inspected typeset radicals).
c3(m,k)=0.5*c2(m,k), and c4(m,k)=c2(m,k)+2*c1(m,k). (PDF p. 4, anchor: numbered equation (2), visually inspected typeset radicals).

The condition and every conclusion are indexed by k=1,...,n, with A_k denoting the first k columns and R_k,Q_k the corresponding partial factors. (PDF p. 4, anchor: Theorem 1, condition (3) and conclusions (4)-(8)).

Both condition (3) and bound (7) contain kappa_2(R_k)^2, not an unsquared condition number and not kappa_2(A_k). (PDF p. 4, anchor: Theorem 1, condition (3) and conclusions (4)-(8); anchor: paragraph after Theorem 1 and Remark 1).
higher_order_terms: The paper explicitly adopts a first-order convention and treats O(epsilon_M^2) as making no significant contribution. (PDF p. 3, anchor: IEEE floating-point model and linear approximation).

Theorem 1 qualifies the entire collection of equations (4)-(8) as holding to within O(epsilon_M^2), although the displayed inequalities do not append an explicit remainder term. (PDF p. 4, anchor: Theorem 1, condition (3) and conclusions (4)-(8)).
The proof of equation (7) contains a quadratic Delta A_k term and ends with the stated first-order coefficient plus O(epsilon_M^2). (PDF p. 14, anchor: Appendix proof of equation (7)).
exceptional_values: The explicit rounding formula is restricted to results in the normalized range. (PDF p. 3, anchor: IEEE floating-point model and linear approximation).

The selected passage gives no separate treatment of subnormal results, overflow, infinities, or NaNs beyond the normalized-range qualification. (PDF p. 3, anchor: IEEE floating-point model and linear approximation).

Algorithm 2 contains square roots of psi_k-phi_k and psi_k+phi_k and division by r_kk, but the pseudocode states no explicit guard for a negative square-root argument or zero divisor. (PDF p. 3, anchor: Algorithm 2 (CGS-P)).
The paper states that condition (3) assures nonsingularity of R. (PDF p. 4, anchor: paragraph after Theorem 1 and Remark 1).

undebatable_constraints: The exact second branch of c1 is 2*sqrt(2)*m*k+2*sqrt(k); it is not 2*sqrt(2*m*k)+2*sqrt(k). (PDF p. 4, anchor: numbered equation (2), visually inspected typeset radicals).
The loss-of-orthogonality conclusion is ||I-Q_k^T Q_k||_2 <= c4(m,k)kappa_2(R_k)^2 epsilon_M. (PDF p. 4, anchor: Theorem 1, condition (3) and conclusions (4)-(8), equation (7)).
The conditioning hypothesis is the strict inequality c4(m,k)epsilon_M*kappa_2(R_k)^2 < 1 for every k. (PDF p. 4, anchor: Theorem 1, condition (3) and conclusions (4)-(8), equation (3)).

The theorem concerns computed factors from Algorithm 2, CGS-P, not standard Algorithm 1, CGS-S. (PDF p. 3, anchor: Algorithm 2 (CGS-P); PDF p. 4, anchor: Theorem 1, condition (3) and conclusions (4)-(8)).
The bound is expressed using kappa_2(R_k), not kappa_2(A_k), and the condition number is squared. (PDF p. 4, anchor: paragraph after Theorem 1 and Remark 1).

The enclosing theorem is multi-part: equations (4), (5), (6), (7), and (8) are all conclusions under the same hypothesis and first-order convention. (PDF p. 4, anchor: Theorem 1, condition (3) and conclusions (4)-(8)).
The inherited matrix setup is real, rectangular with m >= n, and full column rank. (PDF p. 2, anchor: standing rectangular full-rank setup immediately before equation (1)).

ambiguities.issue: The displayed theorem suppresses rather than explicitly quantifies the second-order remainder.
ambiguities.evidence: The theorem says equations (4)-(8) hold to within O(epsilon_M^2), while the displayed inequalities omit additive remainder terms. (PDF p. 4, anchor: Theorem 1, condition (3) and conclusions (4)-(8)).
ambiguities.impact: A formal contract must either represent an explicit second-order remainder or state that it is modeling the paper's first-order truncation.

ambiguities.issue: Condition (3) is written using an inverse-based condition number before nonsingularity is discussed.
ambiguities.evidence: The paper defines kappa_2(R_k)=||R_k||_2||R_k^(-1)||_2, assumes condition (3), and then says condition (3) assures R is nonsingular. (PDF p. 4, anchors: Theorem 1, condition (3) and conclusions (4)-(8); paragraph after Theorem 1 and Remark 1).
ambiguities.impact: A formalization must make the invertibility needed to define kappa_2(R_k) explicit or use a condition-number convention defined for singular matrices.

ambiguities.issue: The identity matrix in equation (7) is not subscripted.
ambiguities.evidence: Equation (7) prints I-Q_k^T Q_k; Q_k^T Q_k is k-by-k from the algorithmic dimensions. (PDF p. 3, anchor: Algorithm 2 (CGS-P); PDF p. 4, anchor: Theorem 1, condition (3) and conclusions (4)-(8)).
ambiguities.impact: Its dimension is forced to be k-by-k, but a formal statement must supply that dimension explicitly.

ambiguities.issue: The selected passage does not specify failure behavior for the square roots and divisions in CGS-P.
ambiguities.evidence: Algorithm 2 computes sqrt(psi_k-phi_k), sqrt(psi_k+phi_k), and v_k/r_kk without a displayed guard, while the numerical model is stated only for normalized-range results. (PDF p. 3, anchors: Algorithm 2 (CGS-P); IEEE floating-point model and linear approximation).
ambiguities.impact: A formalization must decide whether successful normalized execution and valid square-root arguments are implicit preconditions or require explicit hypotheses.

contract_plain_english: For a real full-column-rank m-by-n matrix A with m >= n, run the computed pythagorean classical Gram-Schmidt Algorithm 2. (PDF p. 2, anchor: standing rectangular full-rank setup immediately before equation (1); PDF p. 3, anchor: Algorithm 2 (CGS-P)). If, for every prefix k, c4(m,k)epsilon_M*kappa_2(R_k)^2 < 1, then to first order in epsilon_M all five conclusions (4)-(8) hold. In particular, the computed Q_k loses orthogonality by at most c4(m,k)kappa_2(R_k)^2 epsilon_M in the matrix 2-norm. (PDF p. 4, anchor: Theorem 1, condition (3) and conclusions (4)-(8)). The coefficient is c4=c2+2c1, with c1(m,k)=2*sqrt(2)*m*k+2*sqrt(k) for k>=2; visual inspection confirms that sqrt(2) does not extend over m*k. (PDF p. 4, anchor: numbered equation (2), visually inspected typeset radicals).
